extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, and those seeking a concise encyclopedia-style profile of The Atlantic magazine
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedic entry describing the history, ownership, editorial focus, format, controversies, and corporate structure of The Atlantic magazine and its related properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial focus / topics
rubrics_metrics.description: The Atlantic "features articles on politics, foreign affairs, business and the economy, culture and the arts, technology, and science."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aims at serious national readers and 'thought leaders'; publishes longform journalism and newsmaker interviews. Examples of influential cover stories include Anne Marie Slaughter's "Why Women Still Can't Have It All" and Ta-Nehisi Coates's "A Case for Reparations." Use of longform reporting and analysis is a core editorial signature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication frequency and format
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically published monthly (1857–2000) and at various frequencies since; since 2003 published 10 per year, and it announced it will resume publishing monthly issues in 2025.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Print frequency has changed over time; the magazine drops/changes cover branding (dropped 'Monthly' in 2004). Frequency affects issue planning, editorial calendar, and special-issue strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscription / paywall model and access rules
rubrics_metrics.description: As of 2025 the website is a four-tier freemium model. Paid subscribers get access to unlimited articles; base paid model is 'Digital', 'Print & Digital' includes physical copies, and 'Premium' subscription includes advertisement-free access. Historically: paywall removed in 2008, soft limitations introduced in 2016, and a new paywall trials/relaunch culminating in metered and later stricter limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access rules have included limiting free readers to first two paragraphs, limiting number of free articles per month, treating adblock users differently, and tiered pricing (historical examples: $49.99 digital, $59.99 print & digital, $100–120 premium). Subscription model decisions shape audience reach and revenue strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial standards, fact-checking, corrections, and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Atlantic has issued retractions and editor's notes when it "cannot attest to the trustworthiness and credibility of the author." Legal filings and a defamation suit highlighted "fact-checking and ethical concerns" and led to removals, corrections and clarifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances (e.g., retraction of Ruth Shalit Barrett article; settlement and corrections around Molly Ball's piece) show requirements for robust fact-checking, transparent corrections/retractions, and editorial processes that can be scrutinized legally and publicly. Editorial accountability includes publishing editor's notes and making corrections; inability to vouch for sources/authors can require retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponsored content and advertising transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: In January 2013 the website published 'sponsor content' promoting David Miscavige that looked like articles; this was widely criticized, later removed, and an apology issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clear separation between advertising/sponsored content and editorial content; avoid publishing advertorials that mimic editorial pieces. Failure to distinguish led to reputational harm and public criticism in this example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment moderation and separation of editorial/marketing roles
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 2013 sponsor-content incident, "The page comments were moderated by the marketing team, not by editorial staff, and comments critical of the church were being removed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment moderation should be aligned with editorial standards and ethics; assigning moderation to marketing rather than editorial can create conflicts and perceived censorship. Policies should be explicit about moderation responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative and longform impact
rubrics_metrics.description: The Atlantic has "emerged in the 21st century as an influential platform for longform storytelling and newsmaker interviews," publishing cover stories that sparked broad discussion (examples: Vannevar Bush's 'As We May Think' influencing hypertext development; Anne Marie Slaughter; Ta-Nehisi Coates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial aims include producing narrative, investigative, and longform pieces with public impact; such pieces may influence policy and cultural conversation and thus require rigorous sourcing and narrative craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimedia and video production
rubrics_metrics.description: The Atlantic created a video channel and Atlantic Studios, evolving from an aggregator to an in-house production studio that creates custom video series and original documentaries (example: released the documentary 'White Noise').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content production extends beyond text to video and documentary formats; standards for multimedia production involve different workflows, editorial oversight, and production resources compared to print/online articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Events and conferences (Aspen Ideas Festival)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Atlantic and the Aspen Institute launched the Aspen Ideas Festival in 2005, a ten-day event featuring 350 presenters, 200 sessions, and 3,000 attendees; it is described as a 'political who's who'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hosting and curating events is part of the brand's activities; event programming standards (speaker selection, session quality, diversity of perspectives) affect reputation and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Networked properties and vertical expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Atlantic has launched and operated multiple web properties and verticals (The Atlantic Wire / The Wire, TheAtlanticCities / CityLab, CityLab Latino, Health Channel) and experimented with aggregation and standalone sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expansion into verticals and separate properties implies editorial specialization and different audiences; strategic choices include whether to integrate or spin off verticals and how to staff them. Past outcomes include rebranding, folding back into the main site, and sales (e.g., CityLab sold to Bloomberg).

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards and recognition as quality signal
rubrics_metrics.description: The periodical was named Magazine of the Year by the American Society of Magazine Editors (2016) and its writers have won Pulitzer Prizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry awards and prizes are cited as signals of editorial quality and influence; they can be used as benchmarks for assessing impact and prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial stance and political endorsements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Atlantic's editorial board has historically made political endorsements (e.g., endorsed Abraham Lincoln in 1860, Lyndon B. Johnson in 1964, Hillary Clinton in 2016, Joe Biden in 2020) and has taken explicit editorial positions (e.g., calls for impeachment of Donald Trump).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The magazine's editorial voice can include endorsements and advocacy; such positions shape audience perception and may invite public controversy. Transparency about editorial positions and the distinction between news reporting and editorial opinion are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership and leadership influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Ownership changes (e.g., sale to David G. Bradley in 1999; majority stake acquired by Laurene Powell Jobs's Emerson Collective in 2017) and editorial leadership changes (list of editors-in-chief, move of offices to Washington, D.C.) are documented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporate ownership and senior leadership decisions (publisher, editor-in-chief, CEO) influence editorial direction, staffing, and strategic choices (e.g., move of offices, paywall strategy). Readers and analysts may evaluate editorial independence and direction in light of ownership changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal risk and reputational management
rubrics_metrics.description: The Atlantic faced legal action (e.g., defamation and invasion of privacy claim in Japan over Molly Ball's article leading to removals, corrections, clarifications, and a settlement) and other lawsuits such as the Ruth Shalit Barrett defamation suit which was settled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigorous legal review, sourcing, and editorial processes are necessary to manage defamation and privacy risk. Legal settlements, retractions, and public editor's notes are part of reputational remediation; these episodes highlight the consequences of editorial lapses.
